comments.author: @RolandPihlakas
comments.text: 15-20 years ago Google had Google Desktop search. It was good. Now it is long defunct as well. Even though it was installed locally, it is still not available anymore!

Notebook LM is a one-way street. Wes says it himself: Google will ultimately discontinue it. It looks like a weekend project of one of their engineers. And it's also not really a second brain when you're not able to really organize your stuff but only drop a bag of documents into a RAG search. I use Logseq as a second brain. Well organized, you can find most with the built-in full-text search and personal discipline. If anything, something like this needs to be an open source tool (for privacy) where you configure multiple text, knowledge and document sources (maybe even including LLM tools that can query a database). Basically your own private search engine with RAG and tools to aggregate all your little second brains (Logseq/Obsidian, your browser bookmarks, some file system folder or WebDAV directory, your CRM database etc.). I'm pretty sure that there are multiple open source tools that go into this direction. It would be better to look at those.

comments.author: @brianmi40
comments.text:
This field is called Knowledge Management or Personal Information Management.  

I've been fascinated by and pursuing it both personally and professionally, dating back to the release of InfoSelect, a "personal information manager" in 1986 on PCs touted by a respected expert at the time Steve Gibbs, author of Spinrite (1987) which famously was the first user tool to do low level hard drive error testing and block out areas of the hard drive before they would fail.

I also implemented two different knowledge management systems for the PC Help Desks I managed.  One an internal tool in 1996 that let us store text and linked docs in a searchable knowledgebase that was shared by all the Help Desk agents.

Then in 1999 as the Internet was taking off I was featured in articles in PC Week and Service News for adopting an early Web tool called "Web Advisor" at my company which let you build a knowledgebase within it, and even supported "clarifying questions" which you could associate with any knowledge in order to get the person needing guidance down to the correct support article you had published in it.  For example, if you searched for "how to set print margins", our clarifying question would offer: "Which Microsoft application do you need help setting the margins in?" and would then offer the list of Word, Excel, Powerpoint...  to lead you to the specific steps to follow for each, including screenshots.  We had managed to replace a full time person with the volume of questions that were being serviced through the tool to our users at the brokerage firm.  I even had a full time person curating the knowledge and adding new guidance into it for all our in-house apps the brokers used.  Pretty cool for 1999.

InfoSelect is still a useful tool today (albeit over priced I think in today's world for what it does).  But if you just want local fast retrieval of anything from a bunch of freeform notes it's still hard to beat 40 years later and is dirt simple to use.  You enter ANY text, image, or Web link into resizeable "notes" on the screen.  At any time after, you can press "g" (for GET) and start typing any word or text.  It IMMEDIATELY (seriously) displays all notes you have that contain that letter and continues filtering them out, the more you type.  So when I press an "I" lots of notes, all with an I appear, but then adding an "n" afterwards, only notes with "In" appear and as I continue to type the rest of the word "Interpreter" then ONLY the notes I have with that word in totality within it will appear, and I've, for example, found my note(s) about "Open Interpreter".

LOTS of PC tools have competed in this space over the years.  I've gotten a lot of use out of RightNote as I like it's Tabs you create and name for organization, which then each support a custom folder hierarchy you can construct to organize all your data you enter into it, giving custom names to each and any "node" of that (folder or entry below a folder) which can then contain any information out on the full screen to the right that displays the contents therein.  It has full text search, so similarly, searching for "Interpreter" will show all you entries with that text, and you can click on each one at a time in the results list.  So I can have a Tab named "AI Tools", then in that a folder called "RAG tools", and then unlimited entries under that for any info I want to store on RAGs, whether graphics including screenshots, copied in or typed text and attachments that are links to any files.  So, for example, you could enter a brief summary and then a file attachment, and then searches can see the summary content, show you the entry and you can open the file.  It just doesn't see what's in any attachment directly to search.

Then for full documents to be able to search them directly, there's a decent tool like EverDoc, which lets you add documents into it's folder structure and it will then scan them for content which you can then do full text searches on.  It's sort of like Paperport which was released in 1985 and supported organizing lots of PDF files, however EverDoc supports more document types than just PDFs, and can even OCR things somewhat in graphics formats, so that you can search for the text appearing in those images, but I haven't tested it very much.  EverDoc is getting a bit dated as all these tools are now in an AI centric world.  I kind of wish they had higher aspirations for it and were updating it to enable something like LLM searches and chats with the content.  But it does seem to work, and is a local tool so no data risks and no subscription model as a one time buy.

In the AI world, the category of these tools is called "RAG" (retrieval augmented generation).  Oversimplified simply think of it as an LLM specifically pointed at a folder of your documents that it scans, and like your test of Notebook LM lets you query the LLM for answers that will be in the documents.  Lots of corporate interest in these tools today as, for example, an Insurance company, or HR department can store all their policy docs and info and anyone can AI query or chat for anything stored there.

These have an advantage over tools like Notebook LM as they store the documents locally, and aren't at the risk of a company like Google abandoning it (and your data all disappears!) or a smaller company trying to carve out a niche and going under (same data result!).  There are obviously privacy concerns whenever considering to upload your documents online.

The tools like Lobechat and LM Studio which seem to be among the top easiest tools for novices to get an AI running at home, don't currently support RAG add ins, however, they have discussed doing so in their forums.  Perplexity just indicated there's a tool called "anythingLLM" that can enable a RAG in something like LM Studio, but I haven't investigated it or searched for alternatives.

The challenges that all these tools and systems create for users includes the age old question of: "what do I need to have a COPY OF myself, and what can I TRUST will still be OUT THERE and I can just link to it"

For example, many might not know that you can hi-lite any text (sentence, paragraph...) on any Web page and then Right Click and have the option to get a link to THAT VERY HI-LITE on that page.  Useful, for example, here if I wanted to point you to a quote or specific text on a page, and not just the page itself.

So, you have to decide, is that PDF (or any info) critical to have available in the future, so I'll pull it down and store it on my disk space and somehow be able to reference it (EverDoc or a RAG or just attachment in a PIM like RightNote...).  How import it is to you to be able to quickly or definitely put your finger on that information in the future will likely guide your decision.  If it's not that critical, the decision may be to just live with a Google search or AI like Perplexity which does great Web searches directly from it's Chrome add in in order to retrieve it in the future along with the risk that it's aged out or deleted from the Internet and gone.

As a somewhat knowledge management crazed guy, I'm certainly excited about what RAGs can do with an LLM and looking forward to one really floating to the top to be dead simple to get going in order to leverage LLMs to manage and let us chat with all the personal knowledge we want, we're surely close to such a tool being put out if I'm not already just unaware of a great one!

comments.text:
Here are some ways the AI assistant in Notebook LM could help manage and organize various aspects of your life:

• Knowledge Management - By uploading documents, research papers, meeting notes, etc. into Notebook LM, you essentially create a personalized knowledge base that the AI can quickly search through and synthesize information from. This allows you to easily access and connect ideas across different sources.

• Task and Project Planning - You can feed the AI details about your current projects, to-do lists, schedules, etc. and then query it for next actions, priorities, deadlines and it can provide an organized view leveraging all that contextual data.

• Writing and Analysis - The AI can assist with writing tasks like reports, emails, presentations, and papers by summarizing relevant information from your sources. It can also analyze complex topics and break them down.

• Research Assistance - When exploring a new topic, you can upload source materials and have the AI extract key insights, identify knowledge gaps, suggest additional readings, etc.

• Idea Generation - Prompt the AI with a broad topic and it can creativity combine concepts from your personalized data sources to generate new ideas and thought-starters.

• Memory Aid - Rather than trying to memorize everything, you can offload information to your Notebook LM and rely on the AI to resurface relevant details when you need them.

The key advantage is having an AI system tightly integrated with your personal information sources to serve as an extension of your own memory and analysis capabilities. This could significantly boost productivity, learning, and creativity across all domains of your life.
